analysis.title: Housing Starts Bounced Back in October, But Underlying Activity Remains Weak
key_insights: Total housing starts rose 9.9% in October to an annualized 1.309 million units after three straight monthly declines. They were up 2.8% year over year and above PNC's forecast of 1.270 million.
September starts were revised down to 1.191 million from 1.221 million. The three-month moving average fell 1.6% to 1.260 million units.

Single-family starts rose about 4% and multifamily starts about 25% in October. Single-family starts were still 3.2% below a year earlier, while multifamily starts were more than 20% higher. Multifamily is considerably more volatile month to month.
Regionally, starts rose 49% in the Midwest and 11% in the South, and the Midwest gain was driven entirely by multifamily. Starts fell 21% in the Northeast and 3% in the West.

Building permits, a leading indicator, fell 7.4% in October to an annualized 1.295 million units. Single-family permits fell 8.7% and multifamily permits fell 5.3%. Total permits were down 8.7% from a year earlier.
Completions rose 6.5% in October but were 10.4% below a year earlier. PNC expects them to drift lower as the pipeline of homes under construction shrinks and starts stay subdued.

PNC expects homebuilding to stay subdued into 2027 because mortgage rates are elevated and affordability is poor. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate is about 7.1%, and new-home sales and prospective buyer traffic have softened.
The NAHB Housing Market Index remained near a 15-year low in November, pointing to continued weak builder sentiment. PNC sees growing downside risk to single-family construction.
Permits fell sharply in July and August, and PNC says this suggests starts will stay under pressure in coming months.
Starts peaked near 1.8 million units in April 2022 as mortgage rates rose from below 3% to above 7%. PNC says the downtrend that began in 2022 remains intact.

sector_views.rationale: PNC expects homebuilding to remain subdued into 2027 given elevated mortgage rates and poor affordability, with single-family construction facing growing downside risks.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The rebound followed three monthly declines and beat PNC's forecast, but the three-month average still fell.
The downward revision lowers the base for the October gain.
Permits are a leading indicator, and the decline points to pressure on starts ahead.
Completions are trending lower since the August 2024 peak.
The elevated rate restrains housing demand.

risk_factors: A prolonged Middle East conflict could keep energy prices and mortgage rates elevated.
Renewed deterioration in the labor market would weigh on homebuyer demand and construction.
Single-family construction faces growing downside risks.
Permits fell sharply in July and August, which points to pressure on starts.
geopolitical: A prolonged conflict in the Middle East could keep energy prices elevated and put upward pressure on mortgage rates.
Uncertainty over tariffs and the conflict in the Middle East has made housing starts volatile since early 2025.

tension_points.bull_case: The labor market has stabilized in 2026, which should support housing demand, and October starts beat PNC's forecast.
tension_points.bear_case: Mortgage rates near 7.1%, poor affordability, softer new-home sales and buyer traffic, permits down 8.7% y/y and a near 15-year low in builder sentiment point to continued weakness.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Renewed labor market deterioration or a prolonged Middle East conflict that keeps energy prices and mortgage rates elevated would worsen the outlook.
